Chapter 1: Childhood Interrupted by War and the Loss of Home
You know, there’s a special rhythm to childhood—a kind of safety and comfort we often take for granted. Imagine a small village in Sierra Leone, where kids spent their days drumming, dancing, and soaking up stories from elders under big, shady trees. The world felt wide open, but never really threatening. The future? It seemed limitless. And the past was just a tapestry of family memories and local traditions.
But then, war crept in and shattered everything. At first, it was just whispers—rumors of violence in towns far away. But one day, those distant echoes turned real. Gunfire replaced the laughter of children. Families scrambled, grabbing whatever they could, never knowing if they’d ever come back. Suddenly, the familiar felt foreign.
Picture a group of boys, who used to be all about music and school, now forced to run for their lives. They moved from village to village, always just a step ahead of the chaos. Hunger quickly became a constant companion. The boys learned to read the world differently—looking for abandoned homes, the smell of smoke, or the eerie silence that meant danger had passed through. Their entire world shrank down to just two things: the next meal, and a place to sleep where they felt even a little bit safe.
Losing a home isn’t just about losing four walls and a roof. It’s about losing your place in the world—losing that sense of where you belong. These boys clung to each other, forming a sort of makeshift family. But even that was fragile. Trust was hard to come by. Every new face could mean danger. War has a strange way of turning neighbors into strangers.
As days turned into weeks, their memories of old lives started to blur. The stories they used to share—about their families, their dreams—began to feel like distant fairy tales. War demanded their full attention. All that mattered was survival.
Still, even in all that fear and uncertainty, small acts of kindness stood out. Maybe a woman in a village would share a handful of rice, or an old man might offer a place to rest for the night. Little moments like that reminded the boys that not everyone had changed. There were still people who remembered what it meant to be human.
But the war didn’t let up. Every time they thought they’d found safety, violence caught up to them. The sound of gunfire, the sight of burning homes, people fleeing in terror—this became their new normal. The boys learned to move quietly, to hide at the slightest sign of trouble, to trust only those who proved themselves over time.
Losing innocence wasn’t something that happened all at once. It was slow—a little bit more each day. New challenges, new reasons to be afraid. These boys grew up fast, not because of birthdays, but because survival demanded it. They had to push aside their feelings and just focus on getting through each day. The world was suddenly a dangerous place, and there was no turning back.
Even so, memories of family lingered. Maybe the image of a mother’s smile, the sound of a father’s voice, or the warmth of a sibling’s hug. These memories brought comfort, but also pain. They reminded the boys of what they’d lost, but also of what they were fighting to hold onto—even if it was just in their hearts.
Moving through war-torn villages was a true test of endurance. Hunger gnawed at them, and fear stole their sleep. Still, they kept going—driven by hope that somewhere, somehow, they’d find safety again. The world had changed forever, but their longing for home never left.
